questions.stem: Human rights are best described as:
options: entitlements that each government may choose to give or withhold
basic entitlements that belong to every person because they are human
privileges granted only to citizens who have always obeyed the law
rights that exist only if they are written into a nation's constitution
questions.explanation: Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms every person has simply because they are human, regardless of nationality or conduct. They are recognised, rather than created, by constitutions, statutes and treaties.

questions.stem: Human rights are often described as universal and inalienable. 'Inalienable' means that they:
options: apply only in countries that have signed international human rights treaties
can be sold or transferred to another person if the holder agrees
belong only to adults and not to children or young people
should not be taken away, except in specific situations and by due process
questions.explanation: Inalienable rights cannot be given up or taken away, except in limited situations according to due process, such as a lawful prison sentence limiting liberty. 'Universal' is the separate idea that rights belong to everyone everywhere.

questions.stem: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in:
questions.explanation: The General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948, in the aftermath of the Second World War. The United Nations itself was founded in 1945, and the two major covenants on rights were adopted in 1966.

questions.stem: Why is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights significant?
options: It created the High Court of Australia and set out the court's powers
It lists the express rights that appear in the Australian Constitution
It was the first global statement of the rights that all people should enjoy
It is a treaty whose terms bind Australian courts directly in every case they decide
questions.explanation: The Universal Declaration set out, for the first time, rights that all people everywhere should enjoy, and it has shaped later treaties and national laws. It is a declaration rather than a binding treaty, and it is not part of the Australian Constitution.

questions.stem: Which statement about the legal status of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is correct?
options: It was drafted by the Australian Parliament and passed as a federal statute
It is not itself a binding treaty, but it has influenced later treaties such as the ICCPR
It is binding on Australia and can be enforced directly by any person in any Victorian court
It replaced the express rights in the Australian Constitution after 1948
questions.explanation: The Universal Declaration is a statement of principles, but its rights were developed into binding treaties such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Treaties themselves bind Australian courts only once parliament implements them in legislation.

questions.stem: Australia has ratified the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. For the covenant's rights to be enforceable in Australian courts:
options: nothing more is needed, because ratification makes them law
the High Court must first approve the treaty in a case
a referendum must be passed in every state and territory
parliament must pass legislation that implements them
questions.explanation: In Australia, signing and ratifying a treaty binds the nation internationally, but its terms become enforceable domestic law only when parliament passes legislation. That is why many rights are protected through statutes that implement treaties.

questions.stem: The 1967 referendum is sometimes wrongly believed to have given First Nations people the right to vote. The referendum actually:
options: recognised native title over traditional lands as part of Australian common law
created the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities for all Australian states
allowed the Commonwealth to make laws for First Nations people and count them in the census
gave every First Nations person in Australia the right to vote in federal elections for the first time
questions.explanation: The 1967 referendum removed words from section 51(xxvi) that excluded Aboriginal people from the Commonwealth's race power and repealed section 127, which had excluded them from population counts. All First Nations people had already gained the right to vote federally in 1962, and native title was recognised by the courts in 1992.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an express right in the Australian Constitution?
options: Freedom of speech on any topic
The right to privacy in the home
The right to a free education
Freedom of religion (section 116)
questions.explanation: Section 116 protects freedom of religion from Commonwealth laws. The Constitution has no express right to freedom of speech, privacy or education.

questions.stem: Section 80 of the Australian Constitution provides for:
options: trial by jury for every criminal offence in Australia, state or federal
trial by jury for state indictable offences only
trial by jury for civil claims above $100,000
trial by jury for indictable offences against Commonwealth law
questions.explanation: Section 80 guarantees a jury trial for a person tried on indictment for an offence against a law of the Commonwealth. It does not apply to state offences or to civil claims.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth compulsorily acquires a farm to build an airport. Under section 51(xxxi) of the Constitution, the acquisition must be:
options: approved at a referendum
approved by the Supreme Court
made only with the owner's consent
on just terms
questions.explanation: Section 51(xxxi) allows the Commonwealth to acquire property only on just terms, which generally means fair compensation. The owner's consent is not required.

questions.stem: Section 117 of the Constitution protects people from:
options: discrimination based on their sex or gender
discrimination based on their religion or beliefs
discrimination based on their state of residence
discrimination based on their race or ethnic origin
questions.explanation: Section 117 prevents a state from discriminating against a person because they live in another state. Protection against race and sex discrimination comes from statutes such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth).

questions.stem: Section 116 of the Constitution prevents:
options: any person from publicly criticising the beliefs of a religious group
the Commonwealth from establishing a religion or prohibiting the free exercise of any religion
the Victorian Parliament from passing any law at all that affects religious organisations or schools
private employers from considering an applicant's religion when hiring staff
questions.explanation: Section 116 is a limit on Commonwealth law-making power; it does not bind the states or private individuals. Religious discrimination by employers is dealt with by anti-discrimination statutes.

questions.stem: Why is the protection given by the Constitution's express rights limited?
options: Express rights can be removed by any ordinary Act passed by the Commonwealth Parliament
Express rights can be enforced only by complaining to the Victorian Ombudsman
Express rights apply only to people who were born in Australia
Most express rights restrict only the Commonwealth Parliament, not state parliaments
questions.explanation: Most express rights, such as section 116 and section 80, limit only the Commonwealth, and there are very few of them. They cannot be removed by an ordinary Act, because changing the Constitution requires a referendum.

questions.stem: To change an express right in the Australian Constitution, there must be:
options: a declaration made by the Governor-General acting on the Prime Minister's advice
a referendum passed by a double majority under section 128
a unanimous decision of the full bench of the High Court
an Act passed by both houses of the Victorian Parliament
questions.explanation: Section 128 requires a proposed change to the Constitution to be passed by parliament and then approved by the people at a referendum. The High Court interprets the Constitution but cannot change its words.

questions.stem: In a referendum to change the Constitution, a double majority means:
options: two-thirds of all voters nationally, counted across all states and territories together
a national majority of voters, and a majority of voters in at least four of the six states
a majority of members in both houses of the Commonwealth Parliament voting on the same day
a majority of voters in every one of the six states and both of the mainland territories
questions.explanation: A referendum succeeds only with a majority of voters across the nation and a majority of voters in a majority of states, which is four of six. Territory votes count towards the national total but not towards the majority of states.

questions.stem: The High Court has found that the Constitution contains an implied:
options: right to privacy in the home
right to bear arms for self-defence
right to free public education
freedom of political communication
questions.explanation: The High Court has held that the system of representative government created by the Constitution implies a freedom to communicate about political matters. There is no implied right to privacy, education or bearing arms.

questions.stem: Which statement about the implied freedom of political communication is correct?
options: It protects only political communication by members of parliament while they are in parliament
It limits the power of parliaments to restrict political communication, rather than giving individuals a personal right
It gives every person in Australia an unlimited right to say anything they wish on any topic in public, without any limits
It was written into the words of the Constitution when Australians approved it at a referendum
questions.explanation: The implied freedom operates as a restriction on law-making power: laws that unduly burden political communication can be invalid. It is not an unlimited right to free speech, and it was found by the High Court, not added by referendum.

questions.stem: In Roach v Electoral Commissioner (2007), the High Court held that:
options: each state may decide for itself who votes in federal elections
a law banning all prisoners from voting in federal elections was invalid
every prisoner must be allowed to vote, whatever the length of their sentence
the Constitution contains an express right for every adult citizen to vote
questions.explanation: The High Court found that sections 7 and 24, which require parliament to be 'directly chosen by the people', protect the vote, so a blanket ban on all prisoners voting was invalid. The earlier law, which disqualified prisoners serving sentences of three years or more, continued to apply.

questions.stem: Vicki Lee Roach, a prisoner, challenged a federal law that stopped all prisoners from voting. Her case is an example of:
options: a referendum changing an express right in the Australian Constitution
a tribunal awarding damages to a person for unlawful discrimination
an individual using the courts to influence the protection of a right
parliament creating a new human right by amending the Victorian Charter
questions.explanation: Roach brought a High Court challenge that resulted in the blanket ban being struck down, which shows how individuals can use cases to influence rights protection. No referendum or change to the Charter was involved.

questions.stem: The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities is:
options: a Victorian Act of parliament that protects mainly civil and political rights
a part of the Australian Constitution that can be changed only by a national referendum
an international treaty that was signed by the Victorian Government in 1948
a set of rights that applies to the Commonwealth and to every state equally
questions.explanation: The Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (Vic) is an ordinary Victorian statute that protects rights such as freedom of expression and the right to a fair hearing. It applies only to Victorian laws and public authorities.

questions.stem: Under the Charter, a member of parliament who introduces a bill into the Victorian Parliament must:
options: remove any part of the bill that would limit a right before it is debated
table a statement of compatibility saying whether the bill is compatible with Charter rights
obtain approval from the Supreme Court of Victoria before the bill can be debated in parliament
hold a referendum if the bill would limit any of the rights protected by the Charter
questions.explanation: A statement of compatibility explains whether, and how, a bill is compatible with the Charter's rights. Parliament may still pass a bill that limits rights, so the Charter does not require incompatible parts to be removed.

questions.stem: Which body reports to the Victorian Parliament on whether bills are compatible with the Charter?
options: The Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission
The Victorian Ombudsman
The Scrutiny of Acts and Regulations Committee
The Victorian Law Reform Commission
questions.explanation: The Scrutiny of Acts and Regulations Committee, a parliamentary committee, examines every bill and reports on its compatibility with Charter rights. The Victorian Law Reform Commission recommends changes to the law but does not scrutinise every bill.

questions.stem: Under the Charter, courts must interpret Victorian laws:
options: in line with the Universal Declaration, which overrides any Victorian law
compatibly with human rights, so far as possible consistently with their purpose
in whatever way best protects human rights, even if this defeats the law's purpose
only as parliament explains them in the bill's statement of compatibility
questions.explanation: Section 32 of the Charter requires laws to be interpreted compatibly with human rights where possible, but the interpretation must remain consistent with the law's purpose. Courts cannot rewrite a law to protect rights.

questions.stem: The Supreme Court cannot interpret a Victorian law in a way that is compatible with a Charter right. The court may:
options: declare the law invalid, so that it no longer has any legal effect anywhere in Victoria
order the Victorian Parliament to repeal the law within six months
award damages to the person whose Charter right was limited by the law
issue a declaration of inconsistent interpretation, which does not affect the law's validity
questions.explanation: A declaration of inconsistent interpretation does not invalidate the law, but the relevant minister must respond to parliament in writing within six months. The Charter does not let courts strike down laws or award damages for a breach of a Charter right alone.

questions.stem: Under the Charter, public authorities such as Victoria Police must:
options: pay damages directly to any person whose Charter rights they have limited
ignore Charter rights whenever they are enforcing the criminal law
act compatibly with human rights and properly consider them when making decisions
obtain approval from a court before making any decision that affects a person's rights
questions.explanation: Public authorities must act compatibly with Charter rights and give proper consideration to relevant rights in their decisions. The Charter does not create a separate right to damages for a breach.

questions.stem: Which is a weakness of the Charter as a means of protecting human rights?
options: It gives courts power to strike down any Victorian law that limits rights
It binds the Commonwealth Parliament, which reduces Victoria's control
Parliament can amend or override it, because it is an ordinary Act
It can be changed only by a referendum of all Victorian voters
questions.explanation: Because the Charter is an ordinary statute, the Victorian Parliament can amend it, repeal it or pass a law that operates despite it. Courts can issue only a declaration of inconsistent interpretation, not strike down laws.

questions.stem: The Charter allows a right to be limited when the limit is:
options: applied to a person who is not an Australian citizen
reasonable and can be justified in a free and democratic society
convenient for the government department that is applying the law
supported by a majority of voters in a public opinion poll
questions.explanation: Section 7(2) of the Charter allows rights to be subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. Charter rights belong to all people in Victoria, not only citizens.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of statute law that protects human rights?
options: Section 116 of the Australian Constitution
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth)
Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992)
questions.explanation: The Racial Discrimination Act is an Act of the Commonwealth Parliament, so it is statute law. Mabo is a court decision (common law), and section 116 is a constitutional right.

questions.stem: The Equal Opportunity Act 2010 (Vic) protects people from:
options: defamatory statements published in newspapers and on social media
being tried without a jury when they are charged with an offence
negligent medical treatment in public and private hospitals
discrimination based on attributes such as age, race, sex and disability
questions.explanation: The Equal Opportunity Act makes it unlawful to discriminate on the basis of protected attributes in areas such as employment, education and the provision of goods and services. Defamation and negligence are dealt with by other areas of civil law.

questions.stem: A Victorian law is inconsistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth). Under section 109 of the Constitution:
options: the Commonwealth law prevails, and the Victorian law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency
the Victorian law prevails within Victoria, and the Commonwealth law applies everywhere else in Australia
whichever of the two laws was passed most recently prevails over the earlier law
both laws continue to apply together, and each person may choose which law to follow
questions.explanation: Section 109 provides that where a state law is inconsistent with a valid Commonwealth law, the Commonwealth law prevails. This allows federal anti-discrimination statutes to protect rights against inconsistent state laws.

questions.stem: A strength of protecting rights through statute law is that:
options: parliament can make detailed laws and update them as society's values change
statutes can be changed only by a referendum, so the rights are secure
a statute can never be overridden or repealed by any later Act
statutes are written by judges, who are independent of government
questions.explanation: Parliament can protect rights in detail and amend statutes when values change. The same flexibility is a weakness, because a later parliament can just as easily weaken or repeal those protections.

questions.stem: A person believes they have experienced racial discrimination that is unlawful under Commonwealth law. They may lodge a complaint with the:
options: Victorian Ombudsman
Crime Statistics Agency
Australian Human Rights Commission
High Court of Australia, as a first step
questions.explanation: The Australian Human Rights Commission investigates and conciliates complaints under federal anti-discrimination laws. If a complaint cannot be resolved, it may proceed to the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit and Family Court, not straight to the High Court.

questions.stem: Common law protects human rights through:
options: decisions of judges that establish rights in cases
Acts passed by the Commonwealth Parliament
the express rights in the Constitution
treaties signed by the federal government
questions.explanation: Courts can recognise and protect rights when deciding cases, creating precedents that later courts follow. Acts of parliament are statute law, which is a different source.

questions.stem: In Dietrich v The Queen (1992), the High Court held that:
options: an accused person who represents himself at trial must be acquitted of the charge
a trial for a serious offence may be delayed if the accused cannot get a lawyer through no fault of their own
every accused person has a right to a free lawyer paid for by the state, whatever the offence charged
every accused person must be tried by a jury, whatever the offence they are charged with
questions.explanation: The High Court held that a judge may stay (delay) a trial for a serious offence where an accused who cannot afford a lawyer, through no fault of their own, would otherwise not get a fair trial. The court did not create a general right to a publicly funded lawyer.

questions.stem: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) is significant because the High Court:
options: rejected terra nullius and recognised native title in Australian common law
gave First Nations people the right to vote in federal elections
held that the 1967 referendum had been invalid and had no legal effect at all
created the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities for Victoria
questions.explanation: The High Court rejected the idea that Australia was land belonging to no-one when the British arrived and recognised that native title could survive. Voting rights for all First Nations people had been legislated decades earlier, in 1962.

questions.stem: After the Mabo decision, the Commonwealth Parliament passed the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth). This shows:
options: the Universal Declaration becoming binding law in Australian courts
a complaints body resolving a dispute between two private parties
a court decision leading parliament to pass statute law protecting a right
parliament overturning a High Court decision by holding a referendum
questions.explanation: The Mabo case changed the common law, and parliament responded with a statute setting out how native title would be recognised and protected. This illustrates the relationship between courts and parliament in protecting rights.

questions.stem: A weakness of common law as a means of protecting rights is that:
options: it requires a referendum before a court can recognise any new common law right
it can be overridden by statute, and courts can act only when a case comes before them
it can never be changed once a court has decided a case and created a binding precedent
it applies only in the High Court of Australia and not in any lower state court
questions.explanation: Parliament can abrogate common law rights by passing a statute, and courts cannot protect a right until someone brings a case, which can be costly. Precedents can be changed by higher courts and apply throughout the court hierarchy.

questions.stem: Some people argue that all prisoners should be able to vote, while others argue that people convicted of serious crimes should lose the vote. This is an example of:
options: a conflict between the civil standard and criminal standard of proof
conflicting attitudes about the scope of a human right
a conflict between express and implied constitutional rights
a conflict between the Charter and the Universal Declaration
questions.explanation: People hold differing views about who should hold a right and when it may be limited, which is a key part of analysing any human rights issue. The disagreement is about values, not a legal conflict between two sources of law.

questions.stem: A student argues that Australia needs stronger national protection of human rights. Which proposal would create a new protection at the national level?
options: Asking the Victorian Ombudsman to enforce the Australian Constitution
Asking the United Nations to vote the Universal Declaration into Australian law
A Commonwealth Human Rights Act passed by the federal parliament
Extending the Victorian Charter so that it binds the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: A national charter or Human Rights Act passed by the Commonwealth Parliament is a commonly discussed reform. A Victorian statute cannot bind the Commonwealth, and the United Nations cannot make laws for Australia.

questions.stem: Which is a strength of protecting a right in the Constitution rather than in a statute?
options: The right can be enforced by complaining to the Victorian Ombudsman
The right cannot be removed by parliament alone, because a referendum is needed
The right can be quickly updated by parliament whenever society's values change
The right is set out in great detail and covers every area of daily life
questions.explanation: Entrenched constitutional rights can only be changed by a referendum, so they are protected from a parliament that wants to remove them. Ease of updating is a strength of statute law, not of constitutional protection.
